did_you_know.text: The psalm opens with the title “A Song of Ascents” and compares those who trust in the Lord to Mount Zion, which is described as firm and never shaken.
Trust in the Lord is presented in the psalm not merely as a feeling, but as a state of stability and permanence, like the steadfastness of Mount Zion.
Jerusalem is described as a city surrounded by mountains, and this image illustrates how the Lord surrounds and protects His people.
Divine protection is presented as enduring: “from now until forever”—from the present onward, without limit.
The psalm expresses the hope that the rule of wickedness will not remain over the destiny of the righteous, so that the righteous will not stretch out their hands to wrongdoing.
The verse connects protection from wickedness with moral preservation: removing the rule of wickedness is intended to keep the righteous from being drawn into its ways.
The fourth verse contains a direct request to the Lord: “Do good, Lord, to those who are good and upright in heart”; goodness and uprightness are described as inner qualities of the heart.
The psalm distinguishes between “those who are good and upright” and “those who turn aside to their crooked ways”—those who deviate onto crooked paths.
The psalm’s conclusion contrasts those who practice iniquity with the desire for peace: after the warning against the way of wrongdoing comes the closing blessing, “Peace be upon Israel.”
